title: Checkpoint: Avicenna to Kant
objective: After this level you can trace how medieval and early modern philosophers argued over reason, faith and experience from Avicenna to Kant.
summary: From Avicenna to Kant, thinkers argued over reason, faith and experience, met the same objection about the self twice, and fought over whether causes really cause.

cards.headline: Chapter 2 finale: reason, faith and experience.
cards.body: From a man floating in midair to Kant’s revolution, one question kept coming back: what can reason know by itself, and where do faith and experience come in? Line up the answers.

items.label: Faith and reason
points: Maimonides: say only what God is not
Aquinas: faith goes beyond reason, never against it

items.label: Reason first
points: Descartes: “I am, I exist” survives every doubt
Spinoza: one substance, God or Nature

items.label: Experience first
points: Locke: the mind starts as a blank slate
Hume: every idea copies an impression

cards.headline: The same objection, twice
cards.body: Avicenna’s floating man and Descartes’s doubter both set aside the body and the senses, and both end up certain they exist. The same objection dogs them both: how do you know that the thing that is aware is a self distinct from the body? Not being aware of your body doesn’t show you aren’t one.

cards.headline: Do causes really cause?
cards.body: Al-Ghazali argued that you never see fire burn cotton, only the two together. The same argument is most often credited to Hume, but al-Ghazali made it centuries earlier. Hume added that experience can’t justify “every event must have a cause”. Kant’s answer was new: cause is a concept the mind itself brings to experience.

cards.headline: Chapter 2 complete
learned: How thinkers from Avicenna to Kant argued over what reason, faith and experience can each know.
Why Avicenna’s floating man and Descartes’s “I am, I exist” face the same objection.
How al-Ghazali, Ibn Rushd, Hume and Kant argued over whether causes really cause.
What split rationalists like Leibniz from empiricists like Locke, and how Kant answered both.

questions.prompt: Avicenna to Kant recap: what did Descartes compare his beliefs to?

options.label: A ship being rebuilt plank by plank
options.rationale: His image was about sorting out rotten items.

options.label: A basket of apples, some rotten
A block of veined marble
options.rationale: That’s Leibniz’s image of the mind.

options.label: A blank slate waiting for experience
options.rationale: That’s Locke’s image of the mind.

questions.explanation: Descartes compared his beliefs to a basket of apples: tip them all out, then put back only the sound ones.

questions.prompt: Avicenna to Kant recap: what did Maimonides call the highest praise of God?

options.label: Silence
A long list of God’s qualities
A proof of God’s existence
options.rationale: He spoke of praise, not proof.

options.label: Singing the Psalms aloud

questions.explanation: Since every positive description falls short, Maimonides concluded that the highest praise of God is silence.

questions.prompt: In Avicenna to Kant, how did Kant answer the doubt about causes raised by al-Ghazali and Hume?

options.label: He proved by observation that fire makes cotton burn
options.rationale: Observation was exactly what couldn’t settle it.

options.label: He agreed that there are no causes at all
options.rationale: He held every event we experience has a cause.

options.label: He said cause is a concept the mind brings to all experience
He said only God causes anything
options.rationale: That was one of al-Ghazali’s accounts, not Kant’s.

questions.explanation: Kant made cause one of the concepts the mind supplies, so every event in experience has a cause.

questions.prompt: Avicenna to Kant recap: which objection faces both the floating man and Descartes’s “I am, I exist”?

options.label: Being unaware of your body doesn’t show you aren’t one
Nobody can really imagine floating in the air
Doubt is impossible for humans
options.rationale: Both arguments use doubt or removal of the senses.

options.label: They were written in languages too few could read

questions.explanation: Both find a self certain of its existence with the body set aside; critics say that doesn’t prove the self isn’t the body.

questions.prompt: Avicenna to Kant recap: which pair of thinkers held that all our ideas come from experience?

options.label: Spinoza and Leibniz
Descartes and Spinoza
Maimonides and Aquinas
options.rationale: Their question was faith and reason.

options.label: Locke and Hume

questions.explanation: Locke’s blank slate and Hume’s ideas copied from impressions both put experience first; Spinoza and Leibniz trusted reason.
